namespace functions {

// Get a comprehensive molecular profile including identity (MW), drug-likeness (QED, Lipinski violations), key physicochemical properties (logP, TPSA, HBD, HBA, rotatable bonds, Fsp3, molar refractivity), complexity metrics (Bertz CT, stereocenters), topology indices (Hall-Kier, Kappa, Balaban J, IPC), pharmacophore feature counts (hydrophobic, aromatic, ionizable), and electronic properties (Gasteiger charges, EState indices, HOMO/LUMO gap).
type get_molecule_profile = (_: {
// SMILES string of the molecule.
smiles: string
}) => any;

// Analyze functional groups in a molecule using AccFG. Returns named functional groups with fragment SMILES, attachment points, and atom IDs for structural reasoning. Use this to understand what chemical motifs are present.
type analyze_functional_groups = (_: {
// SMILES string of the molecule.
smiles: string
}) => any;

// Analyze ring topology and aromaticity. Returns per-system descriptions with ring sizes and heteroatom content, ring type counts (aromatic/aliphatic/saturated/heterocyclic), aromaticity metrics, and flags for PAH, macrocycle, spiro, and bridgehead features.
type analyze_ring_systems = (_: {
// SMILES string of the molecule.
smiles: string
}) => any;

// Assess ADME properties: pKa prediction (acidic/basic sites), ionization state classification at target pH, logD estimation, and aqueous solubility. These are causally linked: pKa → ionization → logD → permeability.
type assess_adme_properties = (_: {
// SMILES string of the molecule.
smiles: string,
// Target pH for ionization/logD estimation (default: 7.4).
ph?: number
}) => any;

// Screen a molecule for toxicophores — structural motifs associated with specific toxicity mechanisms. Groups alerts into categories like 'Michael acceptor' (protein-reactive electrophile), 'alkylating agent' (DNA-reactive), 'PAH' (CYP-activated), etc. Each category includes a mechanistic explanation. Also screens against ToxAlerts endpoint-specific patterns covering skin sensitization, mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, reactive metabolite formation, electrophilic reactivity, chelation, and promiscuity. Returns pharmacophore feature counts (donor/acceptor/aromatic/hydrophobe). Use this to identify structural liabilities and understand their toxicological mechanisms.
type screen_structural_alerts = (_: {
// SMILES string of the molecule.
smiles: string
}) => any;

// Find the most similar molecules from the training set using task-aware embeddings. Returns K nearest neighbors with their labels, key properties (MW, logP, TPSA), and functional groups, plus the closest molecule with the opposite label for contrastive SAR reasoning. Includes KNN accuracy metrics (global and local neighborhood). Use this for structure-activity analysis.
type find_similar_molecules = (_: {
// SMILES string of the query molecule.
smiles: string,
// Task name for task-aware retrieval (e.g., 'AMES', 'DILI').
task: string,
// Number of nearest neighbors to retrieve (default: 5).
k?: number
}) => any;

// Remove salts and counterions from a SMILES string, keeping only the largest organic fragment. Use as a preprocessing step before other analyses when the input SMILES contains disconnected components separated by '.' that include inorganic ions (e.g., [Na+], Cl-, etc.).
type remove_salts = (_: {
// SMILES string (may contain salts).
smiles: string
}) => any;

// Predict CYP450 metabolism: returns top 3 ranked metabolites with SMILES, reaction types, and priority scores for Phase 1 (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) and Phase 2 (glucuronidation, sulfation, GSH conjugation). Uses GLORYx (FAME3 SoM + reaction rules) when cached, otherwise SyGMa rule-based metabolite prediction as fallback. 
type predict_metabolites = (_: {
// SMILES string of the molecule.
smiles: string
}) => any;

} // namespace functions<|end|><|start|>user<|message|>Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: The Ames test is a bacterial reverse mutation assay that detects compounds capable of inducing genetic damage. Histidine-dependent Salmonella typhimurium (and sometimes E. coli tryptophan auxotrophs) are exposed to the test compound; mutagenic compounds cause reversion mutations that restore the bacteria's ability to synthesize the required amino acid, producing visible colonies. The test is run both with and without metabolic activation (rat liver S9 fraction) to detect pro-mutagens that require CYP-mediated bioactivation.

Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Direct-acting mutagens are electrophilic species that react covalently with DNA bases — alkylating agents (epoxides, aziridines, nitrogen mustards, alkyl halides), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, acrylates, vinyl sulfones), and acylating agents. Pro-mutagens require metabolic activation: aromatic amines are N-hydroxylated by CYP1A2 to form reactive hydroxylamines/nitrenium ions that form DNA adducts; polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are epoxidized by CYP1A1/1B1 to form diol-epoxides; nitroaromatics are reduced to reactive nitroso and hydroxylamine intermediates. DNA intercalators — large planar polycyclic molecules — can cause frameshift mutations by inserting between base pairs and disrupting replication fidelity.

Structural features associated with mutagenicity: aromatic amines and their acetylated derivatives (especially primary aromatic amines —NH₂ on an aromatic ring), nitroaromatic groups (—NO₂ on aromatic rings — reduced to reactive species), alkylating functional groups (epoxides, aziridines, alkyl halides, nitrogen mustards), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls adjacent to electron-withdrawing groups), aromatic nitroso groups, hydrazines and hydrazides, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons with bay regions (facilitating diol-epoxide formation), and N-nitroso compounds. Features arguing against mutagenicity: absence of electrophilic or DNA-reactive functional groups, absence of aromatic amines or nitro groups, steric shielding of potentially reactive sites, high molecular weight and steric bulk that prevents DNA intercalation or minor groove binding, and the presence of rapid detoxification handles (e.g., carboxylic acids that promote glucuronidation and clearance before DNA damage occurs).
Question: Given a drug SMILES string, predict whether it
(A) is not mutagenic (B) is mutagenic
Drug SMILES: ClC(Cl)=C(Cl)C(Cl)=C(Cl)Cl
Please think step by step and use the relevant tools in your analysis.

Begin by examining the molecular structure; identify the core scaffold, substituents, and any reactive or pharmacologically relevant motifs. Use tools to gather quantitative data about the molecule's properties.

Critically, perform structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis: retrieve similar molecules with known labels and compare them to the query. If the accuracy of the neighborhood is low, focus on the contrastive example (the most similar molecule with the opposite label) and reason about which specific structural differences explain the divergent outcome and whether our task molecule has those structural differences. This comparative reasoning is often more informative than absolute property values alone.

Integrate all lines of evidence — physicochemical properties, functional group analysis, structural alerts, metabolic liabilities, and SAR analogy — into a coherent argument. Use your internal chemistry knowledge as well. Weigh evidence for and against each label explicitly before committing to your prediction.

Then put your final choice, (A) or (B), after "Answer:"<|end|><|start|>assistant
groups.label: (A)

The test is run both with and without metabolic activation (rat liver S9 fraction) to detect pro-mutagens that require CYP-mediated bioactivation.

Mutagenicity in the Ames test arises through several distinct mechanisms. Direct-acting mutagens are electrophilic species that react covalently with DNA bases — alkylating agents (epoxides, aziridines, nitrogen mustards, alkyl halides), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls, acrylates, vinyl sulfones), and acylating agents. DNA intercalators — large planar polycyclic molecules — can cause frameshift mutations by inserting between base pairs and disrupting replication fidelity.

Structural features associated with mutagenicity: aromatic amines and their acetylated derivatives (especially primary aromatic amines —NH₂ on an aromatic ring), nitroaromatic groups (—NO₂ on aromatic rings — reduced to reactive species), alkylating functional groups (epoxides, aziridines, alkyl halides, nitrogen mustards), Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls adjacent to electron-withdrawing groups), aromatic nitroso groups, hydrazines and hydrazides, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons with bay regions (facilitating diol-epoxide formation), and N-nitroso compounds.
